title: The Man Who Sold The Eiffel Tower Twice
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower. Twice.' (May 1925, Victor Lustig forged Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs stationery and hosted six Paris scrap-metal dealers at the Hotel de Crillon)

Encyclopaedia Britannica / Wikipedia, 'Victor Lustig' (claimed the city would tear down the Eiffel Tower for 7,000 tons of scrap iron; convinced Andre Poisson to buy it plus pay a cash bribe, fled to Vienna, then returned weeks later to sell it a second time)

lines.text: In 1925, one con artist sold the entire Eiffel Tower.
lines.caps: In 1925, | one | con artist | sold | the entire | Eiffel Tower.

lines.text: Then came back weeks later and sold it again.
See, Paris newspapers joked the tower cost too much to paint,
so Victor Lustig printed fake government letters,
inviting six scrap dealers to a secret hotel meeting.
Inside a luxury suite, he whispered the big lie:
the city was secretly tearing down seven thousand tons of iron,
lines.caps: the city was | secretly | tearing down | seven thousand | tons | of iron,

lines.text: and picking one buyer for the famous landmark.
One dealer wanted the metal contract so badly
he handed over a suitcase full of cash, plus a bribe.
Lustig jumped on the next train out of France,
waiting for police headlines that never came.
Because the victim was way too embarrassed to tell anyone.
So Lustig bought a fresh ticket right back to Paris,
slapped another price tag on the tower, and cashed in twice.
